news_drafts.headline: Pembrokeshire projects £22.3m gap for 2027-28; council tax premiums bring in £9m a year
news_drafts.lead:
Pembrokeshire County Council's Director of Resources projects a funding gap of £22.3m for 2027-28, according to a report to the full Council on 15 October 2026. The gap is the difference between what the council expects to spend and what it expects to have. The report says it is hoped the figure "will reduce over the coming months".

The council has kept its council tax premiums, which are extra council tax charged on top of the normal bill for second homes and long-term empty properties. Together they bring in £9m a year, and the second homes premium is currently 125%. An appendix says that, as the majority of the funding is directed to the council's budget, continuing a premium "will support closing the anticipated funding gap for 2027-28". Of the funding, 92% is directed to elements of the council's budget relating to affordable housing and community sustainability.

The report on the long-term empty property premium sets out what changing its rate would do. A 25% cut would widen the 2027-28 gap by about £0.2m, and a 25% rise would narrow it by about £0.2m.
news_drafts.paper_title: Council - Council Tax Premium for Long-Term Empty Properties

news_drafts.headline: Pembrokeshire social care overspent £6.521m in the year; council as a whole underspent by £2.0m
news_drafts.lead:
Pembrokeshire County Council's social care services spent £6.521m more than budgeted in the year, but the council as a whole finished £2.0m under budget. Figures in an appendix to the Governance and Audit Committee's papers for 6 October show the overspend was offset by underspends elsewhere.

Children's Services accounts for most of it, with an overspend of £5.649m. Adult Services overspent by £0.872m. Together they make up the £6.521m. The appendix sets out the position in the council's outturn (the actual figures for the year once it has ended, as against what was budgeted).

Other services spent less than planned and covered the gap. Infrastructure underspent by £1.977m, and Education also finished under budget. The net result across the council was the £2.0m underspend. The figures in the appendix are the council's own and are presented by service, with no explanation of the causes of the social care overspends.

news_drafts.headline: Pembrokeshire puts 92% of second homes council tax premium into its budget, with a £23.3m gap for 2027-28
news_drafts.lead:
Pembrokeshire County Council puts 92% of the money raised from its council tax premium on second homes into its general budget, Cabinet papers for 5 October show. The premium is the extra charge the council applies on top of standard council tax for second homes. In 2026-27, £9.008m of it goes to general fund services, the council's main day-to-day spending account.

The money pays for core services, including homelessness (£2.05m), schools (£4.71m) and public realm maintenance. The paper says the premium therefore covers parts of those services that would otherwise have to be paid for from other sources of day-to-day spending.

That matters because the council projects a funding gap of £23.3m for 2027-28, the shortfall between what it expects to spend and what it expects to have. The council's Director of Resources sets out what changing the premium would do to that gap. The paper says: "Based on the current allocation of 92% of the second homes Council Tax premium income to the Council's budget relating to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities, a 25% decrease in the premium would increase the funding gap for 2027-28 by circa. £1.4m". A 25% change in the premium level would move the gap by about £1.4m either way.
news_drafts.paper_title: 5.1 - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - 2027-28 Options for Bridging the Projected Funding Gap (Cabinet Outline)
findings.headline: Officers recommend a further £5.0m be earmarked for prevention projects, on top of £6.0m of ACP bids already committed over the MTFP.
findings.detail: The paper says the prevention activity is intended to slow the rising demand and complexity of social care costs.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund prevention rather than to balance the budget is a choice other councils may face between short-term budget relief and longer-term demand reduction.
findings.figures: £5.0m recommended prevention earmark; £6.0m ACP bids committed over the MTFP
findings.quote: It is recommended that a further £5.0m be earmarked for prevention projects

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - 2027-28 Options for Bridging the Projected Funding Gap (Cabinet Outline)
findings.headline: Schools ISB balances are projected to fall from £3.739m in 2026-27 to £0.637m in 2029-30, then move to an accumulated net deficit.
findings.detail: The paper says any accumulated deficit would need to be funded from other General Fund reserves, reducing the amount available for committed expenditure.
findings.matters: Schools' balances moving to a net deficit that the council would have to fund is a risk other councils with similar school budgets are also watching.
findings.figures: £3.739m Schools ISB balances 2026-27; £0.637m 2029-30; accumulated net deficit by 2030-31
findings.quote: moving to an accumulated net deficit position by

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - 2027-28 Options for Bridging the Projected Funding Gap (Cabinet Outline)
findings.headline: Council deferred its decision on the use of Second Homes Council Tax Premium income to its meeting on 10 December 2026.
findings.detail: The paper states that the current allocation of 92% to the council's budget relating to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities is assumed to continue over the MTFP. Each 1% change in the allocation is worth £0.081m.
findings.matters: Council Tax premium allocations are being decided annually, and a deferred decision leaves a funding source uncertain for other councils that rely on premium income.
findings.figures: £7.5m Second Homes Premium to General Fund (92%); £2.2m Long Term Empty Premium (100%); £0.081m per 1% allocation change

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - 2027-28 Options for Bridging the Projected Funding Gap (Cabinet Outline)
findings.headline: The highest Council Tax option in the paper, 4.99%, is compared with the 5.0% for 2027-28 in the MTFP approved on 20 February 2026.
findings.detail: The MTFP approved on 20 February 2026 included a 5.0% increase for 2027-28 and 7.5% for 2028-29. Each 1% increase is worth £0.958m net of CTRS.
findings.matters: Comparing the options with the increase previously approved in the MTFP shows how far the proposed Council Tax path departs from the plan.
findings.figures: 5.0% MTFP increase 2027-28; 7.5% MTFP increase 2028-29; 4.99% highest option; £0.958m per 1% increase net of CTRS
findings.quote: shown as Option 5 in Table D1 above is 4.99% which is broadly in line with the MTFP

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - 2027-28 Options for Bridging the Projected Funding Gap (Cabinet Outline)
findings.headline: Pembrokeshire's 2026-27 Band D Council Tax is £1,727.96 after a 4.6% increase, the fifth lowest in Wales.
findings.detail: The paper compares Pembrokeshire with the Welsh average and its neighbours, Ceredigion at £1,987.03 and Carmarthenshire at £1,827.61. It states that a 1% increase costs residents less and generates less income than in most other Welsh authorities.
findings.matters: A low Band D rate limits Council Tax income, which is relevant for any council assessing how much revenue it can raise from tax rises.
findings.figures: £1,727.96 Band D 2026-27; 4.6% increase in 2026-27; £1,987.03 Ceredigion; £1,827.61 Carmarthenshire; £1,907.87 AEF SSA; 15.5% increase to reach SSA
findings.quote: remaining there in 2026-27 with a 4.6% increase
